abstract: This analysis projects that generative AI will increase productivity and GDP by 1.5% by 2035, nearly 3% by 2055, and 3.7% by 2075. The study estimates that 40 percent of current GDP could be substantially affected by AI, with peak annual productivity growth contribution of 0.2 percentage points occurring in 2032. Occupations at the 80th-90th wage percentiles face the greatest exposure to AI automation, with approximately half their tasks susceptible to automation, while both the lowest and highest-earning occupations are less exposed. Employment in fully automatable occupations declined 0.75% between 2021-2024.
keyFindings: Generative AI will increase total factor productivity (TFP) and GDP by 1.5% by 2035, nearly 3% by 2055, and 3.7% by 2075.
Approximately 40 percent of current GDP is potentially exposed to automation, with 23 percent of exposed tasks estimated to eventually be automated.

Occupations around the 80th-90th percentile of earnings are most exposed to AI, with around 50% of their work susceptible to automation on average, while highest and lowest-earning occupations are less exposed.
AI's contribution to annual TFP growth will peak at 0.2 percentage points in 2032, then decline as adoption saturates, with a permanent long-run effect of less than 0.04 percentage points.
Employment in occupations fully automatable by AI fell 0.75% between 2021-2024, while employment in jobs with 90-99% automation potential showed significantly slowed growth since 2022.
methodology: Study combines task-based framework from Acemoglu (2024) with projected AI adoption timeline informed by historical diffusion of comparable technologies (PCs, internet, cloud computing, smartphones). Exposure estimates based on Eloundou et al. (2024) classification of tasks, aggregated to 784 detailed occupational categories using SOC classification. Employment and wage data from Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) and American Community Survey, covering 2021-2024. Cost savings estimates derived from seven peer-reviewed studies of real-world AI adoption. AI adoption rates based on Real-Time Population Survey (RPS) and historical technology adoption data. Long-run TFP impact calculated using formula: Long-run percentage change in TFP = GDP share of tasks impacted by AI × Percentage cost savings from AI × Adoption rate.
qualifiers: Authors emphasize considerable caution is required given the early nature of generative AI, with projections based on limited data on AI's initial effects. Analysis does not account for: AI-driven changes in product quality, emergence of new products and labor tasks from AI adoption, or potential feedback effects on innovation and TFP growth. Projections will be updated as more data becomes available. Future developments in AI technology could lead to significant changes in estimates. Suggests employment data in Figure 4 is 'suggestive evidence' rather than definitive. Notes the 1% of jobs fully automatable by AI represents a small share of total employment. Preliminary analysis on federal budget impact.
